title: End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers
authors: Nicolas Carion, Francisco Massa, Gabriel Synnaeve, Nicolas Usunier, Alexander Kirillov, Sergey Zagoruyko

blocks.html: The problem. Suppose you hand a computer a photo of a street and ask ‘where are the objects, and what are they?’ The honest answer is a short list: [dog at (x,y,w,h), person at …, car at …]. That list has no natural order and no fixed length. Yet for years, detectors refused to produce such a list directly. Instead they guessed thousands of candidate boxes, scored every one, and then ran a clean-up pass to delete the duplicates. DETR (DEtection TRansformer) asks a simple question: why not just predict the list?

Analogy. Old detectors are like a person who, asked to count the people in a room, points at every square foot of floor and asks ‘is there a person here?’, getting a noisy yes/no thousands of times, then has to reconcile the overlapping yeses. DETR is like a person who simply looks once and says ‘there are three people, standing there, there, and there.’ It commits to a fixed number of answer slots and fills each slot with one object or with ‘nothing’.

What changes. Classic detectors are full of hand-designed machinery: anchor boxes (a grid of pre-set box shapes used as guesses), region proposals, and a non-maximum suppression (NMS) step that removes near-duplicate detections of the same object. DETR throws all of that out and treats detection as a single problem — directly predict the set of objects, in one shot.

It needs only two new ingredients. First, a set-based global loss that forces unique predictions through bipartite matching, so each ground-truth object is matched to exactly one prediction — no duplicates, hence no NMS. Second, a Transformer encoder–decoder that reasons about all objects and the whole image at once using attention.

DETR ... views object detection as a direct set prediction problem ... removing the need for many hand-designed components like a non-maximum suppression procedure or anchor generation that explicitly encode our prior knowledge about the task.

The payoff. A genuinely end-to-end detector that, despite its simplicity, matches a well-tuned Faster R-CNN on the COCO benchmark — around 42–44 AP (average precision, the standard detection score where higher is better) — and extends cleanly to panoptic segmentation just by bolting on a small mask head. Its main weaknesses, fixed by later work, are slow training (500 epochs) and poor accuracy on small objects.

Context. This 2020 Facebook AI paper landed right after Transformers had conquered language (BERT, GPT) and were starting to enter vision. DETR was the proof that the same attention machinery could replace a whole genre of carefully engineered computer-vision pipelines, and it kicked off an entire ‘DETR family’ of detectors (Deformable DETR, DINO, DN-DETR) that now dominate the field.

pages.title: Why remove the pipeline?
pages.subtitle: The hidden cost of hand-designed components

blocks.html: The problem. Detectors like Faster R-CNN never predict objects directly. They propose a large number of candidate boxes (from anchors or a region-proposal network), classify and refine each one, and then run NMS to collapse the many near-duplicate boxes that inevitably land on the same object. Every one of these surrogate steps carries assumptions and hyperparameters that must be hand-tuned.

Concrete example. Imagine one cat in an image. An anchor-based detector might fire 20 boxes that all roughly cover the cat, each with a confidence like 0.91, 0.88, 0.95…. NMS then sorts by confidence, keeps the top box, and deletes any other box whose overlap (IoU) with it exceeds a threshold like 0.5. Pick that threshold too high and you keep duplicates; too low and you delete a second, genuinely-different cat standing nearby. This single number is a brittle hand-tuned knob — and it is not learned from data.

items: Anchor scales & aspect ratios — you must guess the sizes/shapes of objects in advance.
IoU matching thresholds — how much overlap counts as ‘the same object’ during training.
NMS threshold — a post-processing rule, not part of the network, not differentiable.
Proposal counts & score cutoffs — more knobs that leak prior knowledge into the model.

blocks.html: Why it matters. These components are not just annoying — they are non-differentiable, so you cannot train through them, and they encode human priors that may not fit the data. DETR’s goal is to make detection end-to-end, the way machine translation became end-to-end with sequence-to-sequence models: feed in raw input, get out the final answer, train the whole thing with one gradient.

The core difficulty. A set has no natural order, and the model must avoid emitting two predictions for one object. A naive loss that simply pairs prediction $i$ with ground-truth object $i$ would be meaningless — which prediction is object 1? If two of the $N$ output slots both decide to describe the cat, nothing in a per-slot loss punishes that redundancy. DETR’s answer is a loss that scores the output as a whole and assigns each ground-truth object to exactly one slot via bipartite matching, described next.

Trivia. The phrase ‘direct set prediction’ was not new — it appeared in earlier work on recurrent detectors — but those models predicted objects one at a time and never matched Faster R-CNN. DETR’s contribution was making set prediction competitive by combining the Hungarian matching loss with the parallel Transformer decoder.

pages.title: The set prediction loss
pages.subtitle: Bipartite matching with the Hungarian algorithm

blocks.html: The problem. DETR always outputs a fixed number $N$ of predictions (the paper uses $N=100$), far more than the objects in any normal image. Before we can compute a loss, we must decide which prediction is responsible for which real object — and the leftover predictions must be told to say ‘no object’. This assignment must be one-to-one, because that is precisely what prevents duplicates.

Concrete example. Say an image has 2 real objects (a dog and a ball) and the network emits $N=100$ predictions. We pad the ground truth with 98 copies of the special class $\varnothing$ (‘no object’) so both sides have 100 entries. Now we ask: which one prediction should be matched to the dog, and which to the ball, so that the total ‘cost’ is lowest? The other 98 predictions get matched to $\varnothing$ and are trained to output the no-object class.
The technical detail. We search over all permutations $\sigma$ of the $N$ predictions for the one minimizing the total pairwise matching cost:

Reading it term by term: $\mathfrak{S}_N$ is the set of all permutations of $N$ elements; $\sigma$ is one such permutation, so $\sigma(i)$ says which prediction is assigned to ground-truth slot $i$. $y_i$ is the $i$-th ground-truth object (a class label plus a box), and $\hat{y}_{\sigma(i)}$ is the prediction assigned to it. $\mathcal{L}_{\text{match}}$ scores how badly that prediction fits that object — combining whether the predicted class matches and how close the boxes are. $\hat{\sigma}$ is the cheapest overall assignment.

How it is computed. Naively trying all $N!$ permutations is impossible, but this is the classic assignment problem, solved exactly in polynomial time by the Hungarian algorithm (Kuhn, 1955). It is the same algorithm used to optimally assign workers to jobs. This one-to-one matching is the whole trick that removes duplicates: each real object claims a single prediction, so no two slots are rewarded for describing the same dog.

The matching cost in detail. For a prediction with class probabilities $\hat{p}$ and box $\hat{b}$, the cost of matching it to ground-truth object $i$ (with class $c_i$ and box $b_i$) trades off class confidence against box accuracy:

Term by term: $\mathbb{1}_{\{c_i \neq \varnothing\}}$ is an indicator that is 1 only when slot $i$ holds a real object (we ignore the cost of matching to $\varnothing$ entries). $\hat{p}_{\sigma(i)}(c_i)$ is the predicted probability that the assigned prediction has the correct class $c_i$ — we subtract it, so higher confidence in the right class lowers cost. $\mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}$ is the box-distance term defined below. Note the matching uses the raw probability, not its log, to keep it on the same scale as the box term.

After the optimal assignment $\hat{\sigma}$ is fixed, the network is trained with the Hungarian loss: a negative-log-likelihood classification term over every slot, plus a box loss for the slots holding real objects:

Here every slot contributes a classification loss (including the empty slots, which must learn to predict $\varnothing$), but only the real-object slots contribute a box loss. Because empty slots vastly outnumber objects, the paper down-weights the log-probability of the $\varnothing$ class by a factor of 10 to fight class imbalance — otherwise the model would just learn to say ‘nothing here’ everywhere.

The box term. Box regression with plain L1 loss is biased: the same L1 error means something very different for a tiny box than a huge one. DETR therefore blends L1 with a scale-invariant generalized IoU (GIoU) term:

In words: $\lVert b_i - \hat{b}_{\sigma(i)} \rVert_1$ is the sum of absolute differences between the predicted and true box coordinates (center $x$, center $y$, width, height, all normalized to the image); $\mathcal{L}_{\text{iou}}$ is the generalized-IoU loss, which measures overlap as a fraction and so behaves the same for big and small boxes; $\lambda_{\text{iou}}$ and $\lambda_{\text{L1}}$ are scalar weights balancing the two (the paper uses $\lambda_{\text{iou}}=2$, $\lambda_{\text{L1}}=5$). Using IoU alongside L1 keeps large and small boxes on comparable footing.

Why this design. The matching loss is conceptually the same role NMS played — deduplication — but it now happens during training, is fully differentiable up to the discrete matching step (the matching itself has no gradient, but is recomputed each forward pass), and needs no threshold. The model learns to specialize its slots.

pages.title: The DETR architecture
pages.subtitle: CNN backbone, Transformer, and object queries

blocks.html: The problem this page answers. We have a loss that wants a fixed set of $N$ predictions. What network produces them? DETR’s answer has three parts — a CNN to see, a Transformer to reason globally, and a set of learned ‘query’ slots to read out objects in parallel.

Part 1 — CNN backbone. A standard convolutional network (e.g. ResNet-50) turns the input image $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H_0 \times W_0}$ into a lower-resolution feature map $f \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}$, typically with $C=2048$ channels and $H,W = H_0/32, W_0/32$. A $1\times1$ convolution then shrinks $C$ down to a smaller dimension $d$ (256). Think of this as compressing a $1000\times1000$ image into a $32\times32$ grid of rich 256-dimensional descriptors.

Part 2 — Transformer encoder. The $H \times W$ grid is flattened into a sequence of $HW$ tokens and fed to a Transformer encoder. Its self-attention lets every image location attend to every other location, giving global context that convolutions struggle to reach: a pixel on a dog’s tail can directly ‘look at’ the dog’s head. Because attention is permutation-invariant, fixed positional encodings are added so the model still knows where each token sits in the grid.

Part 3 — Transformer decoder and object queries. This is where detection happens. The decoder takes $N$ learned embedding vectors called object queries — trainable parameters, the same $N$ for every image. Each query is a ‘slot’ that, through cross-attention, looks at the encoded image, and through self-attention, looks at the other queries. It is then decoded into one prediction: a class (possibly $\varnothing$) and a box.

items: Backbone: image → feature map (32× smaller, many channels), then 1×1 conv to $d=256$.
Encoder: 6 layers of self-attention over all $HW$ spatial positions for global reasoning.
Decoder: 6 layers; $N=100$ object queries attend to image features and to each other, in parallel.
Prediction heads: a shared 3-layer feed-forward network (FFN) turns each decoded query into a box, and a linear layer into class logits.

blocks.html: Why queries deduplicate. Because the queries attend to each other in the decoder’s self-attention, they can coordinate to cover different objects — one query effectively learns ‘I’ll take the object on the left, you take the right.’ Combined with the one-to-one matching loss, this is what lets the model avoid firing twice on the same thing without any NMS.

Parallel, not autoregressive. Unlike a language Transformer that emits one token at a time, DETR’s decoder runs all $N$ queries in parallel — every object is predicted simultaneously in a single forward pass. This makes inference fast and the whole system differentiable end-to-end, with no anchors and no NMS.

Trivia — a striking simplicity. The authors famously noted the core method can be implemented in about 50 lines of PyTorch on top of standard library components. The object queries, when visualized, learn an implicit specialization: different queries prefer different regions and box sizes, effectively learning the role anchors used to play — but learned, not hand-set.

pages.title: Matching Faster R-CNN on COCO
pages.subtitle: Headline numbers and the small-object weakness

blocks.html: The question. Does throwing away anchors and NMS cost accuracy? On COCO (the standard 80-class detection benchmark, scored by AP — the higher the better, averaged over IoU thresholds and object sizes), DETR is competitive with a strong, heavily-tuned Faster R-CNN baseline retrained with the same tricks (GIoU loss, longer schedule).

Reading the table. The base DETR with a ResNet-50 backbone reaches 42.0 AP with fewer parameters than Faster R-CNN; the DC5 variant (dilated convolutions in the last stage, for higher-resolution features) and the deeper ResNet-101 push past 44 AP — comparable to the strong baseline overall, with a far simpler pipeline.

The revealing pattern. Look at the size breakdown. DETR is clearly better on large objects (AP₋ large ~61 vs ~56) — its global self-attention easily covers big regions. But it is markedly worse on small objects (~20 vs ~27). The single low-resolution feature map (no multi-scale feature pyramid) and the fixed budget of 100 queries make tiny objects hard to localize. This was the original DETR’s most-cited limitation.

The other cost: training time. DETR needed a punishing 500-epoch schedule (~3 days on 8 GPUs) to converge, versus the ~12–36 epochs typical of Faster R-CNN. The slow convergence comes largely from the bipartite matching being unstable early in training, when slot assignments flip around. Deformable DETR (2021) and later DINO fixed both issues — multi-scale deformable attention for small objects, and improved query designs for fast convergence.

Trivia. A neat ablation in the paper: if you train DETR and then add NMS at test time, AP barely changes for the full model — direct evidence that the set loss already removed the duplicates NMS used to clean up. (NMS does help slightly when the decoder is shallow, before the queries have fully learned to coordinate.)

The bonus result. Because each object query already produces a per-object representation, DETR extends to panoptic segmentation — labeling every pixel as belonging to a specific object instance (‘things’ like cars and people) or a background region (‘stuff’ like sky and road) — almost for free.

How. Take a DETR already trained for detection, freeze it, and add a small mask head: for each query, compute attention maps over the encoder output and upsample them through a small FPN-style network into a binary mask. Each query that produced a box now also produces a mask; a per-pixel argmax over all masks assembles the final panoptic result. The unified design is competitive with specialized panoptic methods of the time.

Interpretability. The attention maps are unusually readable. Visualizing decoder attention shows each object query focusing on the extremities of its assigned object — the paws and ears of an animal, the edges of a box — which is exactly where the boundaries that define a box live. Visualizing encoder self-attention shows it already separating individual instances before the decoder even runs.
DETR can be naturally extended to ... panoptic segmentation, by training a small extension on top of a pre-trained DETR.

Why this matters. Anchor-based detectors are notoriously opaque — thousands of boxes give little insight into why a decision was made. DETR’s one-query-per-object design gives a clean, inspectable story for each detection, which is valuable both for debugging and for trusting the model. This interpretability, plus the single-architecture-many-tasks flexibility, was a big part of DETR’s appeal.

DETR showed that object detection could be reframed as a clean set-prediction problem, solvable end-to-end with a Transformer, deleting an entire genre of hand-engineered components. Even though its accuracy on small objects and its 500-epoch training left clear room to improve, it opened one of the most active research lines in computer vision.

items: Reformulated detection as direct set prediction with a bipartite-matching (Hungarian) loss — no NMS, no anchors, no proposals.
Used a Transformer encoder–decoder with learned object queries to predict all objects in parallel.
Matched a strong Faster R-CNN (~42–44 AP) on COCO with a much simpler, more interpretable pipeline.
Extended to panoptic segmentation by adding a small mask head on a frozen detector.

Inspired follow-ups — Deformable DETR, Conditional DETR, DAB-DETR, DN-DETR, DINO — that fixed small-object accuracy and cut training from 500 epochs to ~12–36, eventually setting state-of-the-art on COCO.

blocks.html: The bigger picture. Together with Vision Transformer (ViT) the same year, DETR was a turning point: it demonstrated that the attention mechanism from NLP was not a language-specific trick but a general architecture for perception. The ‘query’ abstraction — a learned slot that pulls out one structured output — has since spread far beyond detection, into segmentation (MaskFormer), tracking, and pose estimation.
